channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: ‘Wall-to-wall’ map of NYC trees could help cool cities worldwide
item.description: Cornell Chronicle: “Researchers have created an interactive map identifying 1.8 million individual trees in New York City, with a new approach that could optimize the placement of trees for cooling in cities around the world.”

item.title: Special materials from medieval Europe and the early Edo period made available in the Meiji University Digital Archive
item.description: Meiji University: “In July, Meiji University Library made available special materials from medieval Europe and the early Edo period, acquired in academic year 2025 through the Meiji University Library Promotion Fund, via the Meiji University Digital Archive.”

item.title: Thunderbird to flap twice as fast from September
item.description: The Register: “Thunderbird is moving to fortnightly releases to keep pace with Firefox’s accelerated schedule. Mozilla and its subsidiary MZLA updated their flagship apps this week, releasing Firefox 154 and Thunderbird 154, respectively.”

item.title: A new tool for organizing your negatives: Filmaris
item.description: Down the Road: “Rémi built Filmaris around a simple observation: scanning every negative on a roll one by one is slow, and if you only end up printing or sharing a handful of shots, most of that scanning time was wasted. So Filmaris flips the usual order. You scan or photograph your contact sheets first — a flatbed scanner, a light table, even a Print File sleeve shot with your phone all work — and browse those the way you’d browse a roll with a loupe on a light table. Then you scan only the individual frames worth your time.”

item.title: Sick of Constant Pings, They’re Sending Texts at the Speed of Carrier Pigeon
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “A lot of time has gone into speeding up human communication, from the telegram to the Pony Express to shouting loudly from a rooftop. Lately, at least two apps have asked: Was a carrier pigeon the pinnacle?”

item.title: Reverse-lookup service exposed millions of photos of people’s faces
item.description: Ars Technica: “When someone uploads a photo to the people-search tool ClarityCheck, the website has a clear message: ‘Your reverse image search is private and secure.’ New research, though, shows that the website left more than 9 million image files, including photographs of people’s faces, publicly exposed. And a second misconfiguration publicly exposed people’s email addresses and phone numbers.”

item.title: Despite years of confiscations, the Met still holds hundreds of pieces linked to alleged trafficking and looting figures
item.description: International Consortium of Investigative Journalists: “Even after authorities seized more than $95 million worth of antiquities from New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art in recent years, the institution still holds hundreds more pieces linked to alleged looting and trafficking figures, a new analysis by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists has found.”

item.title: UH oral history center receives $538K for Maui projects
item.description: Maui News: “Four grants totaling $538,000 will support University of Hawaii projects recording dozens of oral histories about Lahaina, water, women’s history and the Lahaina Jodo Mission. Researchers say documenting residents’ experiences, cultural knowledge and memories will help preserve Maui’s history for future generations and contribute to the island’s recovery from the 2023 wildfires.”

item.title: Negative social media posts correlated with changes in the brain’s fear network during the COVID-19 lockdown
item.description: PsyPost: “The collective emotional stress of the COVID-19 pandemic may be reflected in how the human brain regulates fear and anxiety. A recent study published in Frontiers in Nuclear Medicine indicates that on days when public social media posts expressed higher levels of negative emotions, brain scans of patients taken on those same days showed reduced activity in areas responsible for emotional regulation. This provides evidence that societal stress can have measurable, wide-reaching neurological effects on vulnerable populations.”

item.title: Row, row, row your Poe! First-ever Edgar Allan Row paddle event at Inner Harbor in October
item.description: Baltimore Fishbowl: “The thing the organizers need to know is just how many Poes will row. It matters not if fast or slow. Bring your friend or bring your foe, there’s little chance it’s called for snow. Though wind may take your new chapeau, the fun will mitigate the blow, as will, perhaps, a nice merlot. Regardless, sense of rhyme or no, the scene will make a fine tableau.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: IMRRC Archives Go Digital
item.description: Society of Automotive Historians: “Motorsports history is hitting the digital track as the International Motor Racing Research Center (IMRRC) expands public access to its extensive archival collections with the launch of CONTENTdm as its official digital collections platform.”

item.title: Uncover Hidden Paper Trails: New Confederate Quartermaster Records Live on Fold3!
item.description: Fold3: “Military service records tell you when an ancestor served, but supply records reveal how they survived. We’ve just added a new collection to Fold3: Atlanta, Georgia, Confederate States of America Quartermaster Department, 1861-1864.”

item.title: Google Trends Gains Explore Maps & Regional Breakdown
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “Google Trends has added two new features this morning, explore maps and regional breakdown.”

item.title: A recent Windows 11 update is causing game crashes and all kinds of other problems
item.description: Engadget: “A recent Windows 11 update looks to be causing some serious issues on some PCs, according to a report by Windows Latest. The update is triggering game crashes, login errors, display issues, system crashes and more.”

item.title: The Open-Source Investigators Reconstructing the Middle East’s Wars
item.description: Wired Middle East: “With war and conflict raging across the region, researchers and journalists are increasingly turning to open-source intelligence (OSINT) to document atrocities and help hold perpetrators to account. From Gaza and southern Lebanon to Syria and Iran, and with some state actors operating without oversight, those working on open-source investigations are documenting war crimes, challenging official narratives and preserving evidence for future accountability.”

item.title: TikTok could let you send friends money via DM
item.description: Mashable: “Bloomberg reports that code in TikTok’s U.S. iOS app suggests it’s developing a peer-to-peer payment system for users. According to the uncovered code, senders will receive notifications regarding the status of their transactions, while receivers will be able to tap a button to accept incoming payments.”

item.title: This Dying Street Fighter II Cart Is A Sobering Reminder That Physical Doesn’t Mean Forever
item.description: Time Extension: “Ownership of the games we play is something that is naturally very close to the hearts of many gamers, and with good reason – billion-dollar companies are a little too fond of pulling access to digital goods, after all. However, it’s always worth keeping in mind that even physical media doesn’t guarantee you’ll have access to something forever; disc rot is a thing, as we all know, and while cartridges are generally more robust and longer-lasting, even they have an expiry date.”

item.title: Hundreds of Fake VPNs Are Flooding the Chrome Web Store
item.description: Lifehacker: “Many of these extensions are free, some are paid, and some even pretend to be from trusted cybersecurity providers to lure users into handing over unrestricted access to their network and browser. This weekend, I dug through Socket’s report to find out exactly what was going on with these apps and how they managed to clear Web Store moderation without getting flagged by Google. I’ll share what I found and offer some tips to help you avoid these fake VPNs.”

item.title: Roblox must make changes after failing to block adults creeping on kids
item.description: Ars Technica: “Despite making changes last fall to help block adults from messaging unknown children, Roblox is still failing to stop adults from creeping on kids in other ways, Australia’s eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, said on Thursday.”

item.title: The anatomy of censorship and propaganda: What Russia’s Wikipedia clone reveals about authoritarian information control
item.description: CEPR: “This column exploits the 2023 cloning of Russian-language Wikipedia and its subsequent rewriting into Ruwiki, a regime-aligned alternative. Comparing the two 1.9 million-article corpora reveals a coherent editorial intervention legitimising Russia’s aggression, suppressing opposition and criticism of state institutions, and promoting traditional values. Rewriting is far more common than outright deletion, suggesting that modern information control works primarily by changing the meaning of familiar topics rather than making them disappear.”

item.title: Inside U-M’s rare program to save ancient texts
item.description: Bridge Michigan: “The Papyrus Conservation Summer Seminar at the University of Michigan is the only one of its kind in the Americas, according to the university. And it’s one of the few in the world designed to convey the best practices for conserving papyrus manuscripts, ancient texts written on rolls or sheets made from the papyrus plant.”

item.title: Samsung Printer Is The Next Frontier Of Minecraft Servers
item.description: Hackaday: “While DOOM remains the undisputed champion of ‘game you play on every piece of hardware’ it seems that the role of ‘game you play on everything just because you can’ is slowly being shifted to Minecraft, as we have yet another Minecraft server somewhere Minecraft has no business being served– in this case, a Samsung Printer.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Which AI Chatbot Did This School Use to Make Such a Ridiculous Map?
item.description: Gizmodo: “You’ve probably seen the story by now. A school in Kentucky sent students home with a bound agenda that included absurd errors clearly made by AI. The periodic table was nonsense. The map of the U.S. lists the state of Illinois as ‘Vitoiis,’ and Kentucky is listed as ‘Venecky.’ There’s an extra planet called Marc, and Saturn is listed as “Sature,” among countless other gibberish errors.”

item.title: Facing a “deluge” from AI, this publication will only take pitches by phone
item.description: NiemanLab: “Whether you’re a reporter or an editor, your inbox has probably seen an influx of pitches, increasingly written with artificial intelligence. They’re likely bad, irrelevant, and annoyingly clogging up your email. But one publication is over it. If you want to write for The Food Section, you’ll have to pick up the phone.”

item.title: Hallucinating history: Korea enlists youth ambassadors to fix AI errors on cultural heritage
item.description: Korea Times: “The glitch is symbolic of a growing challenge for cultural institutions in the digital age and maintaining historical truth as generative AI becomes the world’s default reference tool. To counter these digital distortions, the Korean government, in partnership with a civil diplomacy organization, is turning to tech-savvy youth to audit algorithms and safeguard the nation’s historical identity online.”

item.title: A Data Center Threatened a 17-Year-Old’s Hometown, So She Turned to TikTok
item.description: Teen Vogue: “Seventeen-year-old Sadie Esperanza Cisneros’s viral TikTok video started like so many others do: ‘Come with me…’ she says to the selfie camera, which is held above her head, showing her outfit. She’s wearing a white tee and low-rise jeans; her lashes are bold and freshly glued (a great promo for her lash-tech business). What comes next, though, is what turned her into an overnight sensation: ‘…to protest against data centers at my local city council meeting,’ she finishes.”

item.title: Even small Maine towns are weighing data center bans
item.description: The Maine Monitor: “Several small towns across Maine are weighing temporary bans on data center development as a nationwide backlash against artificial intelligence and Big Tech continues to grow. Larger communities like Bangor quickly passed moratoriums this spring. Fears of data centers are reaching many smaller towns, with several towns in Oxford County that were unlikely to ever see such projects weighing pauses on hypothetical ones.”

item.title: Black Hat and DEF CON are AI conferences now, too
item.description: The Register: “Our cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons spent last week in Las Vegas for the Black Hat and DEF CON security conferences, and at both events there was only one thing on everyone’s mind: AI agents and their growing threat to cybersecurity defenders.”

item.title: Why we should all be worried about AI in elections
item.description: Rest of World: “The more important question is not what happens when AI generates a fake video of a candidate, but what happens when it is embedded in the systems that administer elections themselves — in procurement decisions, biometric voter-verification systems, and data-sharing arrangements. That is where AI’s impact on democracy may prove most profound.”

item.title: Mental Health Workers Say Algorithmic Triage Is Hurting Patients
item.description: Capital & Main: “To understand some of the ways that AI is affecting mental health care, Capital & Main spoke with more than a dozen therapists, clinicians, academic experts and advocates in Wisconsin and California, who said the hasty integration of the technology is eroding patients’ access to timely and appropriate mental health care.”

item.title: OnlyFans investor says it will “never use AI in any capacity to disrupt creators”
item.description: Tubefilter: “OnlyFans‘ newest investor is talking up his future plans for the platform–including promising that it will ‘never use AI in any capacity to disrupt creators.'”

item.title: Are Microsoft’s AI plans being held back by a shortage of chips?
item.description: The Guardian: “The chips are quite small and some can be held in the palm of a hand. They are fundamental to the development of artificial intelligence models – and the world’s biggest technology companies need vast numbers of them to keep ahead. Microsoft is one of them. And, on paper, it seems to have a problem. A Guardian investigation has found an apparent discrepancy between what the company has said about its AI capacity – and the number of advanced AI chips it has in operation.”

item.title: Your AI research is your responsibility — California court sanctions attorney for delegating AI citation verification to paralegal
item.description: Reuters: “On appeal, the central legal questions concerned the trial court’s reduction of compensable attorney hours, its sua sponte exclusion of paralegal fees from the fee award, and the propriety of sanctions the trial court had imposed against Del Biaggio’s ​counsel in connection with a motion for reconsideration. It was in briefing the paralegal-fee issue that Del Biaggio’s attorney, Carlton Floyd, introduced AI-generated content that would prove deeply problematic.”

item.title: 3M Paid Expert Witness $475/Hour to Use ChatGPT to Defend Company in Major Explosion Lawsuit
item.description: Racket Minnesota: “Previous decisions against 3M and Watson Grinding have tallied more than $150 million, and more cases are working through the courts. ‘It’s David and Goliath, no doubt about it,’ Rob Kwok, a lawyer representing plaintiffs, tells ABC13 Houston. Turns out Goliath is relying on expert witness reports generated by ChatGPT.”

item.title: Scientists increasingly depend on ‘black-box’ tools they cannot control or fully understand
item.description: University of Exeter: “As AI becomes more capable and autonomous, this lack of transparency will make scientific findings harder to interpret and verify. This issue extends beyond AI. Many remote sensing products rely on proprietary processing that researchers cannot fully access and verify, while some wildlife tracking devices provide only processed animal locations, while withholding the underlying raw data.”

item.title: Learning Mahjong with AI help
item.description: Invisible Parade: “A number of my dad friends play Mahjong, so I figured this would be a good time to finally take the time to learn to play. I’ve been able to use AI tools in a way that makes learning extremely efficient (at least I think so).” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: New Website Investigates Eugenics in 20th-Century U.S.
item.description: Dartmouth College: “An innovative new website, Eugenic States: A Contextual Archive, uses digital storytelling to preserve and illuminate a disturbing and largely unknown chapter in U.S. history. During the 20th century, more than 60,000 people in the United States were sterilized based on state eugenics laws.”

item.title: 5.0: Laying the foundation
item.description: Mastodon Blog: “Two weeks ago, we shared insights from Mastodon’s first Discovery Week and how it’s informing our roadmap. Today, we’re offering a deeper dive on what’s in store for Mastodon 5.0 – not an exhaustive list of changes, but a glimpse into major decisions and the thoughts behind them.”

item.title: Firefox new release cadence and what to expect
item.description: Mozilla Blog: “Some of you may have heard about this change from the announcement the team shared in early July, but Firefox is moving to a two-week release cycle. The first release on the new cadence is Firefox 155 on September 1, 2026, two weeks earlier than the originally planned September 15 release.”

item.title: Social Media Platforms Are Training Their AI Models on Your Content, but You Can Stop Them (Sometimes)
item.description: Lifehacker: “Even if you find out how your data’s being used, many sites simply don’t offer you the ability to opt out. And of all the ones I looked at, not a single one that trains AI offers an opt-in model. Put simply, if you logged on today, tech companies took that as your consent to be part of their training data. If there is a way to opt out of even some AI training from a social media site, though, you’ll find instructions in our list below, sorted by alphabetical order.”

item.title: The founders of Kick are in the Club as their new platform comes out of beta
item.description: Tubefilter: “After co-founding the virtual casino Stake.com in 2017, Australian entrepreneurs Bijan Tehrani and Ed Craven set their sights on live streaming with the launch of Kick. Now, Tehrani and Craven are diving deeper into the creator world by announcing the official launch of their new platform: Club. Club, true to its name, is a home for superfan communities centered around individual creators.”

item.title: Flight attendants freaked out that Google is buying tons of Spirit employee data
item.description: Ars Technica: “It may sound like a solid plan if you ever flew on Spirit Airlines and interacted with an employee by email or chat. However, Google’s privacy commitments protecting Spirit customers don’t seem to extend to former Spirit workers. Panicked by the deal, former flight attendants are now rushing to object, worried that Google has not agreed to strip confidential information that workers fear could possibly be used by Google or a third party to link them to scrubbed data.”

item.title: YouTube blocks Serbian director Emir Kusturica’s channel, which was co-produced with the Russian state agency Sputnik
item.description: Meduza: “YouTube has blocked ‘My Life’ (Moj život), a channel run by the Serbian film director Emir Kusturica, the Serbian-language service of the Russian state news agency Sputnik said. The channel published videos produced in collaboration with Sputnik’s Serbian-language service. In all, it had 243 videos of Kusturica’s performances, programs, and music. The channel had 30,000 subscribers.”

item.title: TikTok Discovered a Blind, Pale, Worm-Like Fish
item.description: Nautilus: “There are millions of undiscovered species on Earth. In fact, by some estimates, nearly 90 percent of life on our planet hasn’t been formally described by science. Some of these unknown creatures are very small, like insects, others live in hard-to-reach areas, and many are hiding in plain sight. None of them have any kind of social media presence to speak of—except for one: A previously unknown (to scientists) species of blind cavefish that was recently discovered after being caught on TikTok.”

item.title: MicroSD card torture test writes 133 petabytes of data across 351 cards over three years — cards tested to failure reveal SanDisk as the outlier with 6 failures of the 7 tested
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “There are many different options available if you want to buy a microSD card, but which one of these lasts the longest? Tech enthusiast Matt Cole wanted to find out, so he set up a torture rig in 2023 to put various cards through their paces and recently released an update on the status of his project on the r/DataHoarder subreddit. Cole said that he has a total of 351 microSD cards in his collection coming from 52 different brands and 111 unique models.”

item.title: The river otter makes its first appearance in 100 years along the Bronx River
item.description: Gothamist: “Local scientist R.J. Hawkins caught the long, muscular otter on a motion-activated camera fixed on the river on June 23. The Bronx Zoo, which oversees a long-term camera trap monitoring program for wildlife along the Bronx River, confirmed the sighting. This is the species’ first documented appearance there since the early 1900s, according to the Wildlife Conservation Society, which operates the zoo.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: New UF/IFAS App takes guesswork out of choosing the right plants, supporting pollinators and saving water for Floridians
item.description: University of Florida: “The University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS) Florida-Friendly Landscaping Program (FFL) has launched the FFL Plants & Pollinators App, a comprehensive new resource that brings together plant selection, pollinator support, and sustainable landscaping guidance in one easy-to-use platform.”

item.title: Meta Can’t Stop the Avalanche of Content Filmed on Pervert Glasses
item.description: PetaPixel: “After Mosseri personally delivered the news in July, Meta announced that two large pickup artist accounts — pickup artists refer to men who approach women on the street to try and get their contact details — were pulled from Instagram. However, an investigation by Business Insider found that not only was one of those accounts reactivated not long after the news, but dozens of accounts and hundreds of videos delivering similar content remain visible on Instagram; Meta says the large account has been banned again.”

item.title: BREAKING: TikTok Coughs Up $400M to Settle DOJ Children’s Privacy Lawsuit
item.description: Mediaite: “The Justice Department reached a $400 million settlement with TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance, ending a lawsuit accusing the social media giant of illegally collecting children’s personal information without it having to admit wrongdoing or facing further litigation.”

item.title: Walmart finally supporting in-store tap to pay with Google Pay
item.description: 9to5 Google: “Google announced today that tap to pay with Google Pay is coming to Walmart stores in the US. The retailer has historically been one of the lone holdouts against supporting NFC payments. Instead, it wanted customers to use the QR code-based Walmart Pay inside the Walmart app.”

item.title: Pentagon dismisses Stars and Stripes leadership after editor, reporter oppose military interference
item.description: Associated Press: “The Pentagon on Friday fired the editor-in-chief of Stars and Stripes and a top reporter for insubordination after they spoke publicly against any interference by the Defense Department in the military news outlet that has a long history of editorial independence. It was the latest move by an administration that has grown increasingly aggressive toward the news media.”

item.title: Battle is on to preserve legacy of dying Swiss shoe brand Bally
item.description: SwissInfo: “The dedicated archivist is not allowed to give the media more information. The valuable collection and extensive archive are company property. But the future of the heavily indebted shoe store is uncertain. In the 1970s, Bally experienced countless identity crises. CEOs came and went, and the company alternately positioned itself as a luxury brand and a streetwear label. The only constant was its new shoe collections, which appeared year after year.”

item.title: Teen Boys Are Using Meta Glasses to Harass and Bully Girls at High Schools and Middle Schools
item.description: Futurism: “A Futurism review found large numbers of videos recorded at middle and high schools using smart glasses — almost always Meta’s AI Glasses, designed in partnership with the eyewear titan Ray-Ban — and shared to social media platforms TikTok and Instagram. Recordings take place in school hallways, cafeterias, and classrooms, and feature interactions with other students as well as with staff and faculty. Much of the behavior on display is plainly harassment and bullying, often filmed without the subjects’ knowledge or consent and uploaded online to humiliate them further.”

item.title: Amid intense backlash, people are vandalizing Flock surveillance cameras
item.description: NPR: “An increasing number of people are combating the technology in both legal and illegal ways. According to an NPR review of local news reports, Flock cameras have been vandalized in at least 36 states. People have stolen the cameras, sawed them down, crashed into them with cars, covered them in paint and stickers, and shot at them.”

item.title: Orange County’s Acjachemen Nation Maps 10,000 Years of History for Its First Digital Archive
item.description: Culture OC: “Orange County’s Acjachemen Nation, the Juaneño Band of Mission Indians (JBMI), is building a digital archive for the first time. The Acjachemen Nation (pronounced ah-HAWSH-eh-men) originally inhabited what is now Orange County for as long as 10,000 years. The Acjachemen and the Tongva have had a long, complicated history in the region, including their ancestors’ treatment and captivity at the Mission San Juan Capistrano.”

item.title: Twitch Does Not Respect Their Users, So I’m Quitting
item.description: Dallineation: “I have been streaming on Twitch for three years, but have been considering quitting as early as March 2025 when I drafted – but never published – a blog post about my reasons for leaving. I have come close to publishing that post and quitting several time since then. Yet I had always managed to stop myself and feel like the good outweighed the bad when it came to Twitch. But this incident has tipped the scales unfavorably.”

item.title: After almost six decades on the farm, Ken Kesey’s Furthur bus leaves Oregon
item.description: Lookout Santa Cruz: “Furthur — the writer Ken Kesey’s bus, once a blaring DayGlo chariot, Acid Test home rolling on the road with Merry Pranksters in its belly, a counterculture roving hotspot painted in layers according to its passengers’ whims, an icon that went kaput after a 1969 drive to Woodstock and back to Pleasant Hill, then, a piece of metal on a farm, a dugout, a childhood castle, later pushed in a bog to help sell a prank, left behind moss and blackberry tangles, still there when Kesey died and was buried on the same plot of family land, then pulled out and sat in a barn for 20 years, where until recently it stood still, rusted, waiting — has left Oregon.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Historic photographs of Tonga brought to life in new digital collection
item.description: The Coconet: “A remarkable collection of historic photographs capturing Tongan life throughout the 20th century is now available online, offering families across Tonga and the diaspora a chance to reconnect with the people, places and traditions of generations past. The August Hettig Collection, now held by Auckland Council Libraries, features thousands of negatives documenting Tonga from the early 1900s through to the 1970s.”

item.title: A billion searches a year, now built in: Startpage comes to Firefox
item.description: Mozilla Blog: “Startpage is now a built-in search option for Firefox users on desktop in Germany, France, Austria, Switzerland, and the Netherlands. Android and iOS are coming soon. Whether you want to search with Startpage, or another preferred search engine, it’s as easy as opening your search settings, picking a default, and done.”

item.title: A Good Home Needed Urgently for One of the Most Significant Libraries of Housing and Planning in the Country
item.description: Municipal Dreams: “The trustees of the Octavia Hill Birthplace Museum are disposing of its Harry Simpson Memorial Library in September, next month. The collection comprises the largest discrete library dedicated to housing and planning. The museum is located in Wisbech in the north of Cambridgeshire. If your institution may be interested to receive the whole collection please get in touch as soon as possible.”

item.title: ‘Outlier’ Is a New Word-Search Game That Makes Me Feel Smart
item.description: Lifehacker: “We’ve seen daily word searches before (maybe you use our daily Strands hints?), but this one is a bit different. Instead of finding specific words—or the most words—you’re asked to find the rarest words you can.”

item.title: FCC abolishes gigabit speed goal, suggesting it is unfair to slower technologies
item.description: Ars Technica: “The Federal Communications Commission last week eliminated the gigabit speed goal established during the Biden administration and declared that current levels of broadband deployment in the US are acceptable.”

item.title: U-M Clements Library acquires original Revolutionary War-era sermons
item.description: University of Michigan: “The University of Michigan’s William L. Clements Library recently acquired an archive of 192 original sermons written between 1765 and 1780 by a Revolutionary War chaplain. Coinciding with the final years of the First Great Awakening and continuing through the American Revolution, many of Rev. Joseph Bowman’s sermons were delivered to Continental soldiers during the siege of Boston. Particularly of note are sermons Bowman delivered to the army in July 1775 and February 1776, during the early stages of the War for Independence.”

item.title: Little Websites Everywhere.
item.description: Michelle Barker: “Building a website feels old-fashioned these days. How many more websites do I have left in me before the old fire flickers and dies? Is snuffed out. Before making websites is no longer a viable way to earn a living? The web will change drastically within my lifetime, maybe someday soon, indeed it already has. Maybe it really will fizzle out, a graveyard haunted only by bots and crawlers. But I have a hunch that there will be a long tail.”

item.title: Michigan libraries expand beyond books — and walls — by going outdoors
item.description: Bridge Michigan: “Libraries aren’t just places to check out books anymore. Across Michigan, they’re expanding into community hubs, offering outdoor spaces, programs, tools and other services designed to meet the changing needs of the people who use them — and are reading less. One trend: StoryWalks, outdoor paths designed for young children and families to read while enjoying nature in a fun and engaging way.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Take an interactive journey through America’s national parks
item.description: Google Blog: “As we honor the National Park Service’s 110th birthday and celebrate National Park Week, we’re launching a new interactive hub bringing historic heritage and 60 of the nation’s protected natural wonders together under one digital roof. You can explore more than 150 curated exhibitions, 30 virtual tours, and over 500 miles of Street View imagery across iconic National Parks — from the depths of the Grand Canyon to the peaks of Yosemite.”

item.title: Your pots and pans could contain banned chemicals: See which brands are safe
item.description: NBC Chicago: “Nonprofit group Defend Our Health created a database where people can search more than 200 brands to see if what’s in their kitchen has the chemicals that are banned in several states… The database was created by compiling disclosure reports from companies that state whether there is intentional use of PFAS any of its products.”

item.title: SXSW Launching Podcast Festival In 2027
item.description: Deadline: “SXSW is expanding with the addition of a dedicated podcast festival in 2027, festival organizers announced on Tuesday. This positions Podcasts a core element of the SXSW experience, alongside Film & TV, Music, Comedy, and the Innovation Conference.”

item.title: Judge acquits ex-Google engineer of economic espionage in AI secrets case
item.description: Courthouse News: “A former Google software engineer found guilty of stealing proprietary information on Google’s artificial intelligence technology for a Chinese company had part of his conviction tossed Thursday over insufficient evidence.”

item.title: Patreon is changing its algorithm to help smaller creators get discovered
item.description: The Verge: “Patreon has announced a number of new and overhauled features that are designed to ‘build a better network – and a better internet,’ according to CEO Jack Conte. The Patreon roadmap includes discovery algorithm updates, platform and security improvements, and new features for both creators and fans.”

item.title: As YouTube airs Eurovision, TikTok brings back in-house music contest
item.description: Tubefilter: “TikTok introduced Music On Stage last year, when the app introduced its community to an initial cohort of rising musical stars. According to a blog post, Music On Stage’s first go-around generated 8.2 billion impressions while drawing 1.4 million viewers throughout the broadcast of the Global Finals. Some artists featured in Music On Stage, including winner Anyelique Solorio, have built strong followings on TikTok and beyond.”

item.title: Belfast nuclear bunker now home to one of NI’s most important heritage collections
item.description: Belfast Live: “A nuclear bunker built in South Belfast during the height of the Cold War is now home to one of Northern Ireland’s most important heritage collections. The new archive facility for the Historic Environment Record of Northern Ireland (HERoNI) was opened this week at the former Belfast War Room in Mount Eden Park, Belfast.”

item.title: Open Heritage in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
item.description: Creative Commons: “CHIs [Cultural Heritage Institutions] understand that, as a representation of who we are, heritage helps define our shared humanity and that providing access to heritage generates numerous benefits for society. As such, CHIs, as stewards of trustworthy information imbued within knowledge and culture, have a crucial role to play in growing and protecting the commons and enabling uses that benefit humanity.”

item.title: X’s Algorithm Feeds Off Ragebait and Impacts Democrats More, Study Finds
item.description: 404 Media: “X’s algorithm learns what you hate and shows you more of it, according to a new study just published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS). The paper, titled Value misalignment of X’s feed algorithm is a reflection of value tensions in engagement, found that the site’s algorithm prioritized engagement above all else when it generated a user’s For You Page. It also showed that X serves more ragebait to people who say they are Democrats, although the exact reason for that is unclear.”

item.title: Using Data Analysis to Untangle a 75TB Digital Preservation Problem
item.description: Digital Preservation at the University of Cambridge Libraries and Archives: “For over two decades starting in 2000, the Streaming Media Service (SMS) served as the primary platform for managing and delivering audio and video content across the University. When the service reached its end-of-life in late 2025, the entire system — including its underlying PostgreSQL database and associated media files — was exported to AWS S3 storage for long-term appraisal and selection.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Arkansas launches universal application portal for state colleges and universities
item.description: Arkansas Advocate: “Thirty-four public universities and colleges, and eight private schools, are currently accepting applications submitted through the ACCESS Portal, according to its website. The portal will communicate provisional admissions decisions to the students, as well as financial aid information.”

item.title: Announcing The 2026 Hackaday Retrocomputing Challenge
item.description: Hackaday: “We’re happy to announce the 2026 Hackaday Retrocomputing Challenge! Now’s the chance to put your retrocomputer project up for all to see. Open up a Hackaday.io project that features your retrocomputer project, and we’ll pick our three favorites for a $150 gift certificate courtesy of this contest’s sponsor, DigiKey. You have until Tuesday, October 27th.”

item.title: Mark Zuckerberg encouraged growth over child safety, ex-Meta executive testifies at trial
item.description: Reuters: “A former engineering director at Meta Platforms (META.O), opens new tab testified on Wednesday that ​CEO Mark Zuckerberg fostered a culture that treated child safety as secondary to growth and engagement on Facebook and Instagram. Arturo Bejar, a vocal critic of Meta’s ‌safety record, made the allegation during his second day of testimony in a landmark trial over claims brought by a coalition of states that could reshape Facebook and Instagram, some of the most popular apps on the planet.”

item.title: YouTube offers creators millions to not work with Netflix
item.description: Bloomberg: “YouTube is offering millions of dollars to popular channels if they upload their videos to the site exclusively for a certain period of time, in an effort to halt Netflix’s pursuit of its biggest stars, according to people familiar with the conversations.”

item.title: Google Officially Launches Pakistan Office in Landmark Digital Expansion
item.description: TechJuice: “Google has formally opened its local office in Pakistan, a move Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and company officials described as a major step toward deepening technology cooperation. The inauguration took place on Tuesday when a Google delegation, led by the Global Affairs Vice President of Google Wilson L White, met Shehbaz at the Prime Ministers House.”

item.title: Australia’s new media bargaining laws put pressure on tech platforms to pay for news
item.description: SBS: “The Australian government passed legislation on Thursday that will force tech giants to pay millions of dollars in levies if they fail to strike commercial deals with local media outlets for news on their platforms.The News Bargaining Incentive taxes the companies 2.5 per cent on their advertising revenues unless they strike agreements.”

item.title: Brussels changes gear on Big Tech enforcement
item.description: Politico: “The fines against Google bring the total bill for breaches of the Digital Markets Act to €1.6 billion — a sum that pales in comparison with the antitrust fines of yesteryear. The EU’s highest court recently upheld a €4.1 billion abuse-of-dominance fine against Google dating back to 2018 — an era when Brussels resorted to brute financial force, in contrast to today’s greater emphasis on regulatory dialogue. Some industry watchers see the reduced penalties as evidence that the EU is giving up on its mission to defend the interests of smaller tech firms against the dominant platforms.”

item.title: Why we give our cats, dogs and other pets social media accounts
item.description: The Conversation: “As a researcher and clinician, I am interested in understanding the bond between people and companion animals. In my recent book for mental health professionals, I explore how companion animals shape human behaviours online. I also examine why people post pet-related content online: to reveal aspects of their personal identities, communicate their values or status and build community for themselves.”

item.title: Florida’s Jellyfish Museum is dedicated solely to the mesmerizing floating predators
item.description: Associated Press: “The private Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach, Florida, just north of Fort Lauderdale, is believed to be the first museum in the United States dedicated solely to the translucent invertebrates, and one of the few such spaces in the world, according to the city and the museum’s founders. It was created by Alex and Yana Yanovsky, who previously developed successful aquariums in Ukraine, including their first jellyfish museum in Kyiv.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Three more NC localities weigh pauses on data centers as developer backs away from Raleigh project
item.description: NC Newsline: “Recent polling shows growing opposition to data centers in North Carolina. That trend is being reflected across the state Monday, with three more cities and counties considering putting data project developments on pause, while a proposal to build one in Raleigh was withdrawn Saturday.”

item.title: Exclusive: GOP issues stark warning to AI companies
item.description: Axios: “AI CEOs and top Republicans share in the rising panic. They tell us internal polls show data centers are as popular as spent nuclear waste, and more broadly have become a proxy for feelings about AI.”

item.title: Cherokee Nation bans hyperscale data centers on its lands, won’t support projects without consultation — energy and water consumption, air quality, noise, and cultural resource protection among concerns
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “Cherokee Nation, the largest tribe in the U.S. with more than 475,000 citizens, has banned hyperscale data center development on its tribally owned and trust lands, after a task force convened by Principal Chief Chuck Hoskin Jr. found that 64% of 1,593 surveyed citizens opposed construction of the facilities inside the tribe’s 14-county reservation in northeastern Oklahoma.”

item.title: I didn’t think an ESP32 could run an LLM — until it did
item.description: MakeUseOf: “A developer going by slvDev shipped a project that runs a 28.9-million-parameter model on the same class of $8 chip, at around 9.5 tokens per second, with nothing sent to a server. That’s roughly a hundred times more parameters than Bennett’s model, on similar hardware. What changed is the assumption that every parameter needs to be fast.”

item.title: Binance now lets AI agents trade, but keeping them in check is largely up to users
item.description: TechCrunch: “Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange with more than 300 million registered users, on Thursday launched a platform that lets AI agents analyze markets and execute trades on users’ behalf, bringing autonomous AI directly into the business of managing real money.” Today in “what could possibly go wrong?”

item.title: Cornell Tech’s New Faculty Are Changing How AI Learns, Reasons, and Solves Problems
item.description: Cornell University: “Six new faculty members will join Cornell Tech during the coming year, bringing expertise in artificial intelligence, machine learning, programming languages, and operations research at a pivotal moment for the future of computing. Their work tackles some of the field’s most pressing questions: How can AI systems become more trustworthy, adaptable, and efficient? How can they learn from data more responsibly and sustainably? And how can advances in computing drive breakthroughs across science, industry, and society?”

item.title: Nvidia’s AI moat is shifting from chips to capital
item.description: CNBC: “Following last week’s pact with Wall Street firms to pursue $500 billion worth of financing for Nvidia’s graphics processing units, Nvidia said Monday that it’s providing up to $105 billion for a giant OpenAI data center in Ohio, offering a backstop of sorts should the ChatGPT creator see its fortunes turn.”

item.title: Gov. Josh Shapiro takes a hard line against ‘predatory’ data center developers in Pennsylvania
item.description: NBC News: “Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro announced significant restrictions on data center projects Tuesday, signing an executive order to stop ‘predatory’ backers and ‘bad proposals from infecting our commonwealth.'”

item.title: Opinion | An FT column was condensed with AI. It crossed a novel ethical line.
item.description: Poynter: “Every week seems to bring a new scandal at the crossroads of journalism and artificial intelligence: plagiarism, outright fabrication, em dashes and ‘not this but that’ galore. Using AI to condense a writer’s work, though, is a somewhat novel addition to the genre.”

item.title: Google’s new AI tool helps fact-checkers investigate AI fakes
item.description: NiemanLab: “Every day the fact-checking team for one of India’s largest news organizations works to debunk a slew of false and misleading images circulating across social media. For the six-person team at India Today, that might include addressing an AI-generated archival photograph of a politician, a clip of deadly flooding ripped from its original context, or a full-on deepfake of India’s richest man. Backstory, an experimental tool from Google’s AI research lab, Google DeepMind, is helping India Today sort through this stream of slop, scams, and disinformation.”

item.title: Chatbots Are Pushing Us Toward a Post-Human Internet
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “Depending on whom you ask, bot loops might be banal, dystopian or genuinely useful. No matter how people feel about them, researchers say we’re going to see bot loops much more often as we deputize A.I. systems to do our bidding.”

item.title: Google Search pauses AI-generated images within AI Overviews
item.description: Search Engine Land: “Google has paused an experiment within Google Search to create AI-generated images within AI Overviews for recipe results. Robby Stein, VP of Product at Google, replied to this test minutes ago saying, ‘This was a small experiment we’re no longer running.'”

item.title: Anthropic Explains Its Watermark System as Some Claude Users Loudly Revolt
item.description: Gizmodo: “In a blog post on Friday, Anthropic elaborated on its controversial watermarking system, announced earlier this week as an effort to comply with the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act. Watermarking will make it harder for users to get away with pretending they wrote AI-generated text.”

item.title: Cargo thieves are staging car crashes to steal AI data center hardware
item.description: TechSpot: “Cargo thieves are targeting equipment used in AI data centers, from server switches to cooling systems and networking hardware. In two recent California cases, criminals appear to have used car crashes to separate trucks from their security escorts before the shipments vanished. The incidents highlight how organized groups are using carrier-identity fraud, GPS manipulation and, increasingly, aggressive roadside tactics to steal high-value tech moving through the freight network.”

item.title: Young adults in the U.S. are increasingly wary of AI, concerned it will take jobs
item.description: Pew (PEW PEW PEW PEW PEW!): “Today, 52% of Americans say they are more concerned than excited about the increased use of AI in daily life – up from 37% in 2021. Another 9% are more excited than concerned and 37% say they’re equally excited and concerned, according to a Pew Research Center survey conducted June 22-28, 2026.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Arkansas Department of Agriculture Launches New Active Wildfire Dashboard
item.description: Arkansas Department of Agriculture: “Arkansans can now see where wildfires are burning and how the state is responding, as it happens. The Arkansas Department of Agriculture has launched a new active wildfire dashboard that provides real-time information on wildfires the Department is currently responding to.”

item.title: Legal notices in South Africa now available in a Nuusflits digital archive
item.description: Nuusflits: “Legal notices in South Africa published on Nuusflits can now also be accessed through a dedicated digital archive, giving attorneys, executors, fiduciary practitioners, businesses and members of the public an easier way to view previous legal notice editions in one place.”

item.title: Registration is Now Open For Internet Archive’s Annual Celebration
item.description: Internet Archive Blog: “This year, our annual celebration, ‘Democracy’s Library: Tools for Participation,’ will showcase the many ways people can participate through the Internet Archive—from saving and contributing materials to exploring government records, researching history, and building new tools with our collections and APIs….Our annual celebration is a hybrid event, with an in-person street party at Internet Archive headquarters in San Francisco and a livestream for those joining from afar.”

item.title: Major Update: RVG Discography Is Now “Complete”
item.description: Deep Groove Mono: “For many years the discography was completely missing Verve, CTI, and all the latter-day independent jazz labels [Rudy] Van Gelder recorded for. It brings me great joy to say that everything is now included, and the total number of session dates has ballooned from 1,891 to 3,370.”

item.title: Bluesky says its recent outage was caused by another DDoS attack
item.description: TechCrunch: “Social networking site Bluesky says its recent day-long disruption was caused by a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack that flooded the site with junk traffic. The social network confirmed the incident in a post on Monday, confirming the attack had taken place over the previous 24 hours.”

item.title: The WordPress.com Student Plan Is Here: Give Your Students a Website They Can Keep
item.description: WordPress: “This isn’t a stripped-down classroom version of WordPress.com. The Student Plan includes plugin support, 6 GB of storage, backups, staging sites, SFTP/SSH, phpMyAdmin, and Studio Sync. Students learn and build with many of the same tools they’ll encounter working with WordPress professionally.”

item.title: NEH Grant-Funded Project Will Digitize Pre-Revolutionary War Papers
item.description: Syracuse University: “Two Syracuse University faculty members have received a National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH) grant to digitize portions of the Jeffrey Amherst Papers—a rare, 54-volume trove of 18th-century documents charting British, American colonial and Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy relations in the years surrounding the American Revolution.”

item.title: Facebook, the new jury notice?
item.description: Montana Free Press: “Since the beginning of May, the sheriff’s office has been posting on its Facebook page about once a week the names of county residents who have not responded to their jury-duty summonses. The posts urge people to either respond via a provided link or call the clerk of court, but some comments under the posts (and questions sent to us here at Montana Free Press) raise confusion about the new process, asking why authorities don’t use other forms of communication.”

item.title: A German Court Drew the Piracy Line at 81.5%, KinoGO Was Blocked with (at least) 82.4%
item.description: TorrentFreak: “Germany doesn’t have a hard benchmark for when a site is structurally infringing. However, the site-blocking clearinghouse CUII stated that illegal content clearly outweighs legal content when at least 81.5 percent of a site is infringing. After KinoGO was recently blocked with a floor of 82.4 percent, that line is closing in, raising the question of whether sites could simply pad their libraries with legal fillers.”

item.title: Opinion: Let’s treat our museums and libraries like soccer fields
item.description: City & State New York: “In June, [Mayor Zohran Mamdani] announced that in honor of the World Cup, five soccer fields would keep their lights on all night long, as opposed to the usual 10 p.m. closing time, for six weeks. The results were instantaneous and impactful – more than 4,000 soccer players took advantage of the extension, and communities had newfound safe, gathering places. The next frontier should be libraries and museums – among the city’s most cherished, yet under-leveraged, assets.”

item.title: A researcher at the Old State House discovered slave auctions had once taken place on museum grounds. Her bosses told her to stay silent.
item.description: Arkansas Times: “Wahlquist said she informed her superiors of her discovery, but the reaction was not what she anticipated. ‘They immediately said, “Do not mention this to anyone.” They said to keep researching, but don’t say anything about it because they might be watching.’ ‘They’ were members of the Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders administration, which has made a point of deemphasizing Arkansas’ history of slavery and the state’s treatment of African Americans.”

item.title: A Guide to Personal Data in Archaeological Archives
item.description: Sarah Perry: “The Guide provides basic advice for those working with archaeological data, such as whether the data is personal or sensitive (or both), and how this affects how the data should be handled in different scenarios relating to particular roles. We provide guidance for project managers, field supervisors, post-excavation supervisors, specialists and archivists, and data managers.” Good morning, Internet…
